title: 64-bit computing
summary: 64-bit computing uses 64-bit integers, memory addresses, and processor registers to handle larger data units than 32-bit systems. A 64-bit register can store 2^64 distinct values, enabling direct access to 2^64 bytes (16 exabytes) of byte-addressable memory. While 64-bit processors have existed in supercomputers since the 1970s and RISC workstations since the early 1990s, they entered the mainstream personal computer market in 2003 with x86-64 and PowerPC G5 processors. The primary benefit is the ability to address far more physical RAM than the 4 GB limit of 32-bit architectures, though the full 64-bit address space is rarely utilized in practice.

mechanisms.title: 64-bit processor registers
mechanisms.explanation: Processor registers that are 64 bits wide allow direct support for 64-bit data types and memory addresses. The width of these registers normally limits the amount of directly addressable memory, even if other register types (e.g., floating-point) are wider.

mechanisms.title: 64-bit virtual and physical addressing
mechanisms.explanation: 64-bit computing uses machine code with 64-bit virtual memory addresses. However, not all instruction sets support full 64-bit virtual addresses; for example, x86-64 and AArch64 support only 48 bits, with the remaining 16 bits required to be all zeros or all ones. Several 64-bit instruction sets also support fewer than 64 bits of physical memory address.
